questions.q: A clinical isolate appears deep purple after Gram staining. Which structural feature best explains this result?
choices: A thick peptidoglycan layer that traps the crystal violet-iodine complex during decolorization
An outer membrane rich in lipopolysaccharide that binds crystal violet
A waxy mycolic acid coat that resists the alcohol decolorizer
A polysaccharide capsule that excludes the safranin counterstain
questions.why: Gram-positive cells have a thick, highly cross-linked peptidoglycan wall; alcohol dehydrates and shrinks the pores so the crystal violet-iodine complex stays trapped, leaving cells purple. An LPS-rich outer membrane is the Gram-negative feature, and alcohol dissolves that membrane so the dye washes out, leaving pink cells. Mycolic acid explains acid-fastness (Ziehl-Neelsen), not Gram positivity; mycobacteria stain poorly on Gram. A capsule is unstained by either reagent and appears as a clear halo, not a purple cell.

questions.q: Endotoxin-mediated septic shock in a Gram-negative infection is triggered chiefly by which molecule?
questions.why: Lipid A anchors LPS in the outer membrane and is the toxic moiety; it signals through TLR4/CD14, driving TNF-alpha, IL-1 and nitric oxide release. Teichoic acid is a Gram-positive wall component and is inflammatory but is not endotoxin. Peptidoglycan fragments stimulate NOD receptors but do not produce the classic endotoxin shock syndrome. Flagellin activates TLR5 and drives inflammation, yet it is not the heat-stable endotoxin measured by the limulus assay.

questions.q: During which phase of the bacterial growth curve are cells metabolically active but not yet increasing in number?
questions.why: In lag phase cells synthesize enzymes, ribosomes and metabolites needed for the new medium, so biomass rises while cell number does not. Exponential (log) phase is defined by a constant, maximal division rate. Stationary phase is a plateau where division equals death because nutrients are limiting and waste accumulates. Death phase shows a net logarithmic decline in viable cells.

questions.q: A bacterium grows only in the upper few millimeters of a thioglycolate tube but survives elsewhere. Best classification?
questions.why: Growth in a narrow band just below the surface indicates a microaerophile, which requires oxygen but only at reduced tension because it has limited catalase or superoxide dismutase. An obligate anaerobe grows at the bottom, away from oxygen. A facultative anaerobe grows throughout the tube with densest growth at the top. An aerotolerant anaerobe grows evenly throughout because oxygen neither helps nor harms it.

questions.q: Penicillins and cephalosporins kill bacteria primarily by which mechanism?
choices: Acylating transpeptidases (penicillin-binding proteins) and blocking peptidoglycan cross-linking
Binding the 50S ribosomal subunit and halting peptide bond formation
Inhibiting DNA gyrase and topoisomerase IV
Disrupting the cytoplasmic membrane by inserting into ergosterol
questions.why: Beta-lactams are structural analogs of D-Ala-D-Ala; they covalently acylate transpeptidases, so cross-links fail and autolysins destroy the weakened wall, which is why they are bactericidal only against growing cells. The 50S ribosome is the target of macrolides and chloramphenicol. Gyrase and topoisomerase IV are fluoroquinolone targets. Ergosterol binding describes amphotericin B, an antifungal, and bacteria lack ergosterol entirely.

questions.q: Methicillin resistance in Staphylococcus aureus (MRSA) is conferred by which change?
choices: Plasmid-encoded beta-lactamase that hydrolyzes the beta-lactam ring
The mecA gene encoding PBP2a, a penicillin-binding protein with low beta-lactam affinity
Efflux pumps that export the drug before it reaches the periplasm
Porin loss preventing drug entry through the outer membrane
questions.why: mecA, carried on the SCCmec element, encodes PBP2a; it cross-links peptidoglycan even when all native PBPs are acylated, so every beta-lactam except ceftaroline fails. Classic staphylococcal penicillinase explains penicillin resistance but is defeated by methicillin and nafcillin, so it is not the MRSA mechanism. Efflux is a major mechanism for tetracyclines and fluoroquinolones. Porin loss requires an outer membrane, which S. aureus, a Gram-positive organism, does not have.

questions.q: Which transfer process requires direct cell-to-cell contact through a sex pilus?
questions.why: Conjugation moves plasmid or integrated DNA through a mating bridge built by an F pilus, the main route for spreading multidrug-resistance plasmids. Transformation is uptake of naked DNA from the environment by competent cells and needs no contact. Transduction uses a bacteriophage as the vector. Transposition moves DNA within a single genome and is not a transfer between cells.

questions.q: A retrovirus must carry which enzyme inside the virion for replication to begin in the host cell?
questions.why: Retroviruses copy their plus-sense RNA genome into DNA before integration, and no host enzyme performs that reaction, so reverse transcriptase must be packaged in the virion. A DNA-dependent RNA polymerase is supplied by the host after integration. Neuraminidase is an influenza surface enzyme that releases budded virions. Ribonucleotide reductase is carried by some large DNA viruses to boost dNTP pools, not by retroviruses.

questions.q: Why does influenza cause pandemics rather than only seasonal epidemics?
choices: Antigenic shift by reassortment of its segmented genome creates a surface protein the population has never seen
Point mutations in hemagglutinin accumulate slowly each year
The virus integrates into host DNA and reactivates in waves
It has a double-stranded DNA genome with high mutation rate
questions.why: Influenza A has eight RNA segments; co-infection of one cell allows whole segments to reassort, producing a novel HA or NA against which there is essentially no population immunity, which is the definition of shift and the basis of pandemics. Gradual point mutation is antigenic drift, which causes seasonal epidemics and drives annual vaccine updates. Influenza does not integrate into host DNA; that is a retroviral property. Its genome is negative-sense RNA, not DNA.

questions.q: A latent herpes simplex virus infection resides primarily in which site?
questions.why: HSV travels retrograde up sensory axons and persists as an episome in trigeminal or dorsal root ganglion neurons, reactivating with stress, fever or UV exposure. CD4+ T cells are the latent reservoir for HIV. Hepatocytes host chronic hepatitis B, not HSV latency. Bone marrow progenitors are a latency site for cytomegalovirus, a different herpesvirus.

questions.q: Which feature distinguishes fungal cell membranes and makes them a selective drug target?
choices: Lipoteichoic acid anchored in the bilayer
Ergosterol as the principal membrane sterol
questions.why: Fungi use ergosterol where humans use cholesterol, so azoles (blocking 14-alpha-demethylase) and amphotericin B (binding ergosterol to form pores) are comparatively selective. Peptidoglycan is bacterial; fungal walls are chitin and glucan, the latter targeted by echinocandins. Lipoteichoic acid is Gram-positive bacterial. LPS is Gram-negative bacterial and absent from fungi.

questions.q: A patient from the Ohio River valley has pulmonary nodules, and tissue shows small yeast inside macrophages. Most likely organism?
questions.why: Histoplasma is endemic to the Ohio and Mississippi river valleys, is acquired from bird and bat guano, and its hallmark tissue form is a small intracellular yeast within macrophages. Coccidioides is a Southwestern desert fungus whose tissue form is a large spherule packed with endospores. Blastomyces forms broad-based budding yeast and is extracellular. Cryptococcus is an encapsulated yeast with narrow-based buds, seen with India ink and usually causing meningitis in immunosuppressed hosts.

questions.q: Plasmodium falciparum is transmitted to humans by which vector and stage?
choices: Sporozoites injected by a female Anopheles mosquito
Merozoites injected by an Aedes mosquito
Trypomastigotes deposited in reduviid bug feces
questions.why: The female Anopheles injects sporozoites from its salivary glands; these invade hepatocytes and only later release merozoites that infect erythrocytes. Merozoites are an intra-host stage and Aedes transmits dengue, yellow fever and Zika, not malaria. Waterborne cysts describe Giardia and Entamoeba. Reduviid (kissing bug) feces transmit Trypanosoma cruzi in Chagas disease.

questions.q: Which laboratory result best identifies Staphylococcus aureus and separates it from other staphylococci?
choices: Coagulase positive with beta-hemolysis on blood agar
questions.why: All staphylococci are catalase positive; coagulase activity separates S. aureus from S. epidermidis and S. saprophyticus, and S. aureus is typically beta-hemolytic and golden on agar. Catalase negativity with bile-esculin growth points to Enterococcus. Optochin sensitivity and bile solubility identify Streptococcus pneumoniae. Novobiocin resistance with urease production characterizes S. saprophyticus, a coagulase-negative species.

questions.q: Mycobacterium tuberculosis stains acid-fast because of which wall component?
questions.why: Mycolic acids form a waxy, hydrophobic layer that binds carbolfuchsin so tightly that acid-alcohol cannot remove it, producing the red acid-fast rod. Lipoteichoic acid is a Gram-positive surface polymer without staining significance here. Poly-D-glutamate capsules are the antiphagocytic coat of Bacillus anthracis. Dipicolinic acid stabilizes endospores in Bacillus and Clostridium, and mycobacteria do not form spores.

questions.q: A hospitalized patient on broad-spectrum antibiotics develops profuse diarrhea and pseudomembranous colitis. Which organism and mechanism?
choices: Vibrio cholerae toxin permanently activating Gs and raising cAMP
Shigella toxin cleaving 28S rRNA in colonic mucosa
Enterotoxigenic E. coli heat-stable toxin raising cGMP
Clostridioides difficile toxins A and B inactivating Rho GTPases and disrupting the actin cytoskeleton
questions.why: Antibiotics wipe out competing flora, letting spore-forming C. difficile overgrow; toxins A and B glucosylate Rho GTPases, collapsing the actin cytoskeleton and producing the yellow-white pseudomembranes. Cholera toxin causes massive watery diarrhea without pseudomembranes and is not antibiotic-associated. Shiga toxin produces dysentery and can lead to hemolytic uremic syndrome, again without pseudomembranes. ETEC causes traveler's diarrhea, a self-limited secretory illness.

questions.q: Which antibiotic class inhibits protein synthesis by binding the 30S ribosomal subunit and causing misreading of mRNA?
questions.why: Aminoglycosides bind the 30S subunit, cause misreading and block translocation, and their uptake is oxygen dependent, which is why they fail against anaerobes. Macrolides bind the 50S subunit and block translocation, and they are bacteriostatic. Fluoroquinolones inhibit DNA gyrase and topoisomerase IV, not ribosomes. Glycopeptides such as vancomycin bind D-Ala-D-Ala and block cell wall synthesis.

questions.q: Vancomycin resistance in enterococci (VRE) arises mainly from which change?
choices: Replacement of the terminal D-Ala-D-Ala with D-Ala-D-Lac in the peptidoglycan precursor
questions.why: The vanA/vanB operons remodel the precursor to end in D-Ala-D-Lac, which binds vancomycin about a thousandfold more weakly while still allowing cross-linking. Ribosomal methylation (erm) causes macrolide-lincosamide resistance, not glycopeptide resistance. Beta-lactamases hydrolyze beta-lactams and have no effect on vancomycin, which has no beta-lactam ring. mecA/PBP2a is the staphylococcal methicillin-resistance mechanism.

questions.q: Which cell provides the first specific link between innate recognition and the adaptive response by presenting antigen on MHC class II to naive CD4+ T cells?
questions.why: Dendritic cells capture antigen in tissue, mature, migrate to lymph nodes, and are the only cells that efficiently prime naive CD4+ T cells on MHC II with costimulation. Neutrophils phagocytose and kill but are poor antigen-presenting cells and do not prime naive T cells. NK cells are innate lymphocytes that kill cells lacking MHC I; they present no antigen. Erythrocytes lack nuclei and MHC molecules entirely.

questions.q: Which immunoglobulin class is secreted as a dimer and dominates mucosal surfaces?
questions.why: Secretory IgA is a J-chain-linked dimer with a secretory component that resists proteases, and it neutralizes pathogens in saliva, tears, gut lumen and breast milk. IgM is a pentamer in serum and is the first antibody made in a primary response, but it is not the main mucosal isotype. IgG is the most abundant serum isotype and the only one crossing the placenta. IgE binds mast cell Fc receptors and mediates allergy and antiparasitic defense.

questions.q: A second exposure to the same antigen produces a faster, higher-affinity IgG response mainly because of which process?
choices: Complement fixation by the alternative pathway
Memory B cells that have undergone somatic hypermutation and class switching
Expansion of the innate neutrophil pool
Increased thymic output of naive T cells
questions.why: Germinal center reactions during the primary response generate memory B cells whose receptors have been affinity-matured by somatic hypermutation and switched to IgG, so re-exposure yields a rapid high-titer high-affinity response. The alternative complement pathway is antibody independent and unchanged by prior exposure. Neutrophils are innate and have no antigen memory. Thymic output declines with age and does not mediate the secondary antibody response.

questions.q: Which hypersensitivity type underlies a positive tuberculin (PPD) skin test read at 48 to 72 hours?
choices: Type IV, T-cell mediated delayed hypersensitivity
questions.why: The induration reflects sensitized CD4+ Th1 cells recruiting and activating macrophages, which takes one to three days, the defining timing of type IV. Type I reactions occur within minutes as mast cells degranulate. Type II involves antibody against cell-surface antigens, as in autoimmune hemolytic anemia. Type III involves circulating immune complexes causing serum sickness or vasculitis, typically over one to three weeks.

questions.q: Bacterial endospores survive autoclaving failures because of which property?
choices: A dense capsule that blocks steam penetration
Active efflux of heat-shock denatured proteins
A thick mycolic acid layer around the core
A dehydrated core stabilized by calcium dipicolinate and small acid-soluble proteins
questions.why: The spore core holds very little free water and its DNA is coated by small acid-soluble proteins while calcium dipicolinate stabilizes macromolecules, so spores resist heat, desiccation and chemicals; killing them requires 121 C at 15 psi for 15 to 20 minutes. Capsules are antiphagocytic but not heat protective. Efflux pumps require an active metabolism, and spores are metabolically dormant. Mycolic acid is a mycobacterial feature, and mycobacteria do not sporulate.

questions.q: Which organism is the most common cause of community-acquired bacterial pneumonia and appears as lancet-shaped Gram-positive diplococci?
questions.why: S. pneumoniae is alpha-hemolytic, optochin sensitive, bile soluble, and its polysaccharide capsule is the key virulence factor and vaccine target. Klebsiella is a Gram-negative rod causing currant-jelly sputum pneumonia, classically in alcohol use disorder. Legionella is a faint Gram-negative rod needing charcoal yeast extract with cysteine and iron, often with hyponatremia and diarrhea. Mycoplasma has no cell wall, causes walking pneumonia in young adults, and does not Gram stain.

questions.q: Which of the following explains why a bacteriostatic drug may be preferred over a bactericidal drug in toxin-mediated disease?
choices: Bacteriostatic drugs penetrate cerebrospinal fluid better
Bacteriostatic drugs such as clindamycin halt toxin synthesis without a large burst of lysed bacteria
Bacteriostatic drugs kill faster at the site of infection
Bacteriostatic drugs are unaffected by efflux pumps
questions.why: Protein synthesis inhibitors such as clindamycin or linezolid shut down exotoxin production, and adding them to a beta-lactam in streptococcal toxic shock reduces toxin load rather than releasing it. CSF penetration depends on the individual drug's lipophilicity and protein binding, not on whether it is static or cidal. Bacteriostatic drugs by definition do not kill; they inhibit replication and rely on host immunity. Efflux affects static and cidal drugs alike.

questions.q: In a lytic bacteriophage cycle, what happens immediately after the phage genome enters the bacterial cytoplasm?
choices: The genome integrates into the host chromosome as a prophage
The genome is degraded by host topoisomerase
Host machinery is redirected to transcribe and translate phage early genes
The cell forms an endospore to survive infection
questions.why: In the lytic cycle the phage immediately hijacks host RNA polymerase and ribosomes to make early proteins that shut off host synthesis and start genome replication, ending in assembly and lysis. Integration as a prophage defines the lysogenic cycle instead. Host restriction endonucleases, not topoisomerase, degrade foreign DNA, and successful phages carry modifications that evade them. Sporulation is a starvation response, not an antiviral defense.

questions.q: Which parasite is acquired by ingesting cysts in contaminated water and causes greasy, foul-smelling, non-bloody diarrhea?
questions.why: Giardia trophozoites adhere to the duodenal brush border and cause malabsorptive, fatty, non-bloody diarrhea after hikers or travelers drink untreated water; stool antigen testing is diagnostic and metronidazole treats it. Entamoeba histolytica invades the colon and causes bloody dysentery with flask-shaped ulcers and possible liver abscess. Cryptosporidium causes severe watery diarrhea mainly in advanced HIV and is diagnosed by acid-fast oocysts. Taenia solium is a tapeworm acquired from undercooked pork, not a diarrheal cyst in water.

questions.q: A Gram-negative rod grows on MacConkey agar as pink colonies. What does this indicate?
choices: It ferments lactose, lowering pH and turning the neutral red indicator pink
It is a non-fermenter that oxidizes glucose only
questions.why: MacConkey is selective for Gram-negative organisms via bile salts and crystal violet and differential for lactose fermentation; acid from lactose turns neutral red pink, as with E. coli, Klebsiella and Enterobacter. Hydrogen sulfide production is read as black precipitate on TSI or Hektoen agar, not by pink color. Oxidase status requires a separate reagent test and Pseudomonas, the classic oxidase-positive rod, is a colorless non-fermenter here. Non-fermenters grow as colorless colonies on MacConkey.

questions.q: Which statement about the normal human microbiota is most accurate?
choices: It competitively excludes pathogens and contributes vitamin K and short-chain fatty acids
It is sterile at birth and remains so until weaning
It consists almost entirely of viruses
It is identical in composition at every body site
questions.why: Resident flora occupies adhesion sites, consumes nutrients, produces bacteriocins, and supplies vitamin K and butyrate to colonocytes, which is why antibiotic disruption invites C. difficile and Candida overgrowth. Colonization begins at delivery and is shaped by feeding, so the sterile-until-weaning claim is false. Bacteria dominate by biomass, though a virome and mycobiome exist. Composition differs sharply by site, with anaerobes predominating in colon and staphylococci and cutibacteria on skin.

questions.q: Which mechanism allows Neisseria gonorrhoeae to reinfect the same person repeatedly?
choices: Formation of endospores that persist in tissue
Antigenic variation of pilin and Opa surface proteins
Integration of its genome into host chromosomes
A thick mycolic acid wall preventing antibody binding
questions.why: Gonococci rearrange pilin gene cassettes and vary Opa expression, so antibodies raised against one variant do not neutralize the next, and there is no protective immunity or effective vaccine. Neisseria does not form spores. Genome integration into host chromosomes is a feature of retroviruses and some DNA viruses, not of Neisseria. Mycolic acids belong to mycobacteria; Neisseria is a Gram-negative diplococcus with an LPS-like lipooligosaccharide.

questions.q: Which virus family characteristic explains why antiretroviral therapy suppresses but does not cure HIV?
choices: Provirus integrated into the genome of long-lived resting memory CD4+ T cells
Rapid clearance of virions by neutralizing antibody
Replication restricted to the central nervous system
questions.why: Integrated provirus in resting memory CD4+ cells is transcriptionally silent, so drugs targeting reverse transcriptase, integrase and protease cannot reach it, and viremia rebounds when therapy stops. Neutralizing antibodies are made but the envelope varies too rapidly for them to clear infection. HIV replicates throughout lymphoid tissue, with CNS involvement as one compartment among many. The life cycle is obligately intracellular, which is precisely why latency is possible.

questions.q: Complement activation by the classical pathway is initiated by which event?
choices: Spontaneous hydrolysis of C3 in plasma
Mannose-binding lectin attaching to microbial carbohydrate
C1q binding the Fc regions of antigen-bound IgG or IgM
Properdin stabilizing C3bBb on a bacterial surface
questions.why: The classical pathway begins when C1q engages Fc regions of antibody already bound to antigen, activating C1r and C1s to cleave C4 and C2. Spontaneous C3 tickover starts the alternative pathway. Mannose-binding lectin starts the lectin pathway, which is antibody independent. Properdin stabilizes the alternative pathway C3 convertase and amplifies rather than initiates the classical pathway.

questions.q: Why are patients with terminal complement deficiency (C5 through C9) especially prone to Neisseria infections?
choices: They cannot opsonize bacteria with C3b
They cannot form the membrane attack complex needed to lyse thin-walled Gram-negative cocci
They lack IgA at mucosal surfaces
Their neutrophils cannot generate a respiratory burst
questions.why: C5b through C9 assemble the membrane attack complex, and direct lysis is the dominant defense against Neisseria because their envelope is susceptible to pore formation; recurrent meningococcemia is the classic presentation. C3b opsonization requires C3, which is intact in terminal deficiencies. Selective IgA deficiency predisposes to sinopulmonary and giardial infection instead. Failure of the respiratory burst describes chronic granulomatous disease, which predisposes to catalase-positive organisms.

questions.q: Which sterilization or disinfection method is appropriate for heat-labile plastic surgical tubing that must be sterile?
questions.why: Ethylene oxide alkylates nucleic acids and proteins at low temperature, so it sterilizes including spores without melting plastics, at the cost of long aeration time and toxicity. Autoclaving is the standard for heat-stable items but deforms heat-labile plastics. Boiling kills vegetative cells but not endospores, so it disinfects rather than sterilizes. Alcohol is a fast-acting intermediate-level disinfectant with no sporicidal activity.

questions.q: A child has a sore throat with tonsillar exudate, tender anterior cervical nodes, and no cough. Which organism and why does treatment matter?
choices: Streptococcus pyogenes, because antibiotics reduce the risk of acute rheumatic fever
Epstein-Barr virus, because acyclovir shortens the illness
Corynebacterium diphtheriae, because antibiotics alone neutralize the toxin
Candida albicans, because untreated thrush becomes invasive in healthy children
questions.why: Group A strep meets the Centor criteria described here, and penicillin within nine days of onset prevents acute rheumatic fever, though it does not prevent post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis. EBV causes exudative pharyngitis with posterior nodes and splenomegaly, and acyclovir does not change its course. Diphtheria produces a gray adherent pseudomembrane and requires antitoxin, since antibiotics do not neutralize circulating toxin. Candida causes white plaques that scrape off and rarely invades in an immunocompetent child.

questions.q: Which describes the role of the bacterial capsule in virulence?
choices: It secretes exotoxins into host cytoplasm
It resists phagocytosis by masking surface molecules from opsonins and receptors
questions.why: Polysaccharide capsules block complement deposition and phagocyte recognition, which is why asplenic patients are vulnerable to encapsulated organisms and why conjugate vaccines target capsular antigens. Flagellar anchoring is the job of the basal body in the membrane and wall. Exotoxin delivery into host cells is performed by type III secretion systems. Beta-lactam hydrolysis is catalyzed by periplasmic or secreted beta-lactamases.

questions.q: Trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole is synergistic because the two drugs act how?
choices: Sequential blockade of dihydropteroate synthase and dihydrofolate reductase in folate synthesis
Simultaneous inhibition of the 30S and 50S ribosomal subunits
Inhibition of cell wall synthesis plus inhibition of beta-lactamase
Blockade of DNA gyrase plus blockade of RNA polymerase
questions.why: Sulfamethoxazole is a PABA analog blocking dihydropteroate synthase while trimethoprim blocks dihydrofolate reductase, so two sequential steps of tetrahydrofolate synthesis are hit and the combination becomes bactericidal. Human cells take up preformed folate and use a DHFR with far lower drug affinity, which provides selectivity. Neither drug touches ribosomes, cell walls, gyrase or RNA polymerase.

questions.q: Which statement about prions is correct?
choices: They are small RNA viruses lacking a capsid
They are misfolded proteins that template conversion of normal PrP-C to the beta-sheet-rich PrP-Sc form
They replicate using a DNA intermediate
They are killed reliably by standard autoclave cycles
questions.why: Prions carry no nucleic acid; the pathogenic beta-sheet isoform induces normal cellular PrP to refold, aggregate and produce spongiform change, as in Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease. They are not viruses and carry no RNA genome. With no nucleic acid there is no DNA intermediate and no reverse transcription. They resist routine sterilization, requiring extended autoclaving at 134 C with sodium hydroxide, which is why neurosurgical instruments are often discarded.

questions.q: Which vaccine type generally produces the strongest and most durable cell-mediated immunity but is contraindicated in pregnancy and severe immunosuppression?
questions.why: Live attenuated vaccines such as MMR and varicella replicate briefly, engaging MHC class I and generating cytotoxic T cell memory, but that replication creates a theoretical risk of disease in pregnancy and immunodeficiency. Inactivated vaccines cannot replicate, give mainly humoral immunity and need boosters. Toxoids produce neutralizing antibody against toxin only. Unconjugated polysaccharide vaccines give T-independent responses that are poor in children under two and generate little memory.

questions.q: A wound culture grows an oxidase-positive, non-lactose-fermenting Gram-negative rod producing blue-green pigment in a burn patient. Most likely organism?
questions.why: Pseudomonas aeruginosa is an oxidase-positive aerobic non-fermenter producing pyocyanin and pyoverdine with a grape-like odor, and it is a classic burn wound, ventilator and cystic fibrosis pathogen. E. coli is oxidase negative and ferments lactose. Proteus is a swarming, urease-positive, non-lactose fermenter but is oxidase negative and produces no blue-green pigment. Serratia produces a red pigment and is also oxidase negative.

questions.q: Two carriers of an autosomal recessive allele have a child. What is the probability the child is an unaffected carrier?
questions.why: An Aa by Aa cross yields 1 AA : 2 Aa : 1 aa, so heterozygous carriers are 2 of 4, or 1/2. The 1/4 figure is the chance of being affected (aa) or of being homozygous normal. 3/4 is the chance of being unaffected by any genotype, which includes AA. 2/3 is the carrier probability only after conditioning on the child being known unaffected, which this question does not state.

questions.q: A pedigree shows affected males in every generation, no male-to-male transmission, and all daughters of affected males affected. Which inheritance pattern?
questions.why: An affected father passes his single X to every daughter and his Y to every son, so all daughters are affected and no sons are, the signature of X-linked dominance. Autosomal dominant inheritance would allow father-to-son transmission. X-linked recessive disease appears mostly in males with skipped generations through carrier mothers, not in all daughters of affected men. Mitochondrial inheritance comes only from the mother and affects both sexes.

questions.q: A woman with a mitochondrial disorder has four children. Which statement is correct?
choices: Only her sons can be affected
Only her daughters can transmit it further
All of her children can inherit it, and severity varies with heteroplasmy
None of her children will inherit it if the father is unaffected
questions.why: Mitochondria come from the oocyte, so every child of an affected mother can inherit mutant mtDNA, and the proportion of mutant versus normal genomes (heteroplasmy) plus tissue threshold effects explain the variable severity. Sons can be affected but cannot transmit, so a sons-only claim is wrong. Daughters alone transmit, but that is transmission, not who can be affected. The father's genotype is irrelevant because sperm mitochondria are eliminated.

questions.q: Huntington disease shows earlier onset in successive generations, especially with paternal transmission. This phenomenon is called:
questions.why: Anticipation is earlier onset and greater severity across generations, caused here by expansion of the CAG trinucleotide repeat during spermatogenesis. Incomplete penetrance means some genotype carriers show no phenotype at all. Variable expressivity means the same genotype produces different severity, without the generational trend. Pleiotropy means one gene affects multiple unrelated traits, as in Marfan syndrome.

questions.q: A man with blood type AB and a woman with type O have children. Which blood types are possible?
questions.why: The father contributes either I-A or I-B and the mother contributes i from her ii genotype, so offspring are I-A i (type A) or I-B i (type B). Type AB requires both I-A and I-B, and the mother can supply neither. Type O requires two i alleles, and the father has none. Because I-A and I-B are codominant with i recessive, all four types are not possible from this cross.

questions.q: In a population at Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium, an autosomal recessive disease affects 1 in 10,000 people. What is the carrier frequency?
questions.why: q squared equals 1/10,000 so q is 0.01, p is about 0.99, and carriers are 2pq, roughly 0.0198, or about 1 in 50. The 1 in 100 figure is q itself, the allele frequency, not the carrier frequency. 1 in 200 halves rather than doubles pq. 1 in 5,000 mistakenly doubles the disease frequency instead of computing 2pq.

questions.q: Which condition would violate Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium assumptions?
choices: Random mating with respect to the locus
Consistent selection against the homozygous recessive phenotype
Absence of migration into or out of the population
questions.why: Hardy-Weinberg requires no selection; selection against a genotype changes allele frequencies each generation. Large population size is an assumption because it minimizes genetic drift. Random mating is explicitly required, since assortative mating shifts genotype but not allele frequencies. No migration is required because gene flow introduces alleles at different frequencies.

questions.q: A newborn has a single palmar crease, hypotonia, an endocardial cushion defect, and upslanting palpebral fissures. Karyotype most likely shows:
choices: Trisomy 21, usually from maternal meiosis I nondisjunction
questions.why: This is Down syndrome; about 95 percent of cases are free trisomy 21 arising from nondisjunction in maternal meiosis I, with risk rising sharply with maternal age. 45,X is Turner syndrome, presenting with short stature, webbed neck and coarctation. 47,XXY is Klinefelter syndrome, usually recognized after puberty with tall stature and hypogonadism. Trisomy 18 presents with clenched hands with overlapping fingers, rocker-bottom feet and a very short survival.

questions.q: A phenotypically normal parent carries a balanced Robertsonian translocation involving chromosomes 14 and 21. What is the main clinical consequence?
choices: The parent will develop a chromosome breakage syndrome
Recurrent risk of a child with translocation Down syndrome that does not rise with maternal age
Certainty that all offspring will be affected
Loss of all genes on chromosome 21
questions.why: Robertsonian translocations fuse long arms of acrocentric chromosomes; the carrier is balanced and normal, but unbalanced gametes give offspring with three functional copies of 21q, and that recurrence risk reflects the translocation rather than maternal age. Carriers do not develop breakage syndromes such as Fanconi anemia. Offspring outcomes are a distribution including normal, balanced carrier, unbalanced and nonviable, not universal affection. Only the gene-poor short arms are lost, so no chromosome 21 genes are missing.

questions.q: Deletion of the same region of chromosome 15q11-q13 causes Prader-Willi syndrome when inherited from the father and Angelman syndrome when inherited from the mother. This reflects:
choices: Genomic imprinting, in which expression depends on parent of origin
questions.why: Imprinting silences one parental allele by methylation, so losing the only expressed copy produces disease, and which syndrome results depends on which parent contributed the deletion. Uniparental disomy is one mechanism that can produce these syndromes, not the underlying principle, and it does not explain the deletion cases. Mosaicism means two cell lines within one individual and does not depend on parent of origin. X inactivation applies to X-linked loci in females, not to chromosome 15.

questions.q: Which describes the molecular effect of a frameshift mutation?
choices: A single base change producing the same amino acid
A single base change producing a different amino acid
Insertion or deletion of a number of bases not divisible by three, altering every downstream codon
A change in a promoter reducing transcription rate
questions.why: Frameshifts shift the reading frame, so all downstream codons change and a premature stop codon usually appears, often triggering nonsense-mediated decay and a null allele. A silent mutation changes a base without changing the amino acid. A missense mutation substitutes one amino acid and leaves the frame intact. Promoter mutations are regulatory and alter expression level, not reading frame.

questions.q: In eukaryotic gene expression, what is the function of the spliceosome?
choices: Removes introns and joins exons in the pre-mRNA
questions.why: The spliceosome, built from snRNPs, recognizes GU-AG intron boundaries and the branch point, excises introns as a lariat and ligates exons, and alternative splicing lets one gene yield many proteins. Capping is done co-transcriptionally by guanylyltransferase. Polyadenylation is performed by poly-A polymerase after cleavage at the signal sequence. DNA proofreading is the 3-prime to 5-prime exonuclease activity of DNA polymerase.

questions.q: Which change most directly increases transcription of a eukaryotic gene?
choices: Methylation of CpG islands in the promoter
Histone acetylation that loosens DNA-histone interaction
Binding of a repressor to the operator
questions.why: Histone acetyltransferases neutralize positive lysine charges on histone tails, weakening the grip on negatively charged DNA and opening chromatin for the transcription machinery. Promoter CpG methylation recruits repressive complexes and silences genes. Deacetylation by HDACs restores the positive charge and compacts chromatin. Operator-repressor control is a prokaryotic mechanism illustrated by the lac operon.

questions.q: In the lac operon, lactose induces transcription by which mechanism?
choices: Allolactose binds the repressor, changing its shape so it releases the operator
Lactose binds RNA polymerase and increases its affinity for the promoter
Lactose raises cAMP, which binds the repressor
Lactose directly methylates the operator sequence
questions.why: Allolactose, an isomer of lactose, is the true inducer; it allosterically inactivates the LacI repressor so polymerase can transcribe lacZ, lacY and lacA. Lactose does not bind RNA polymerase. cAMP rises when glucose is low and binds CAP, not the repressor, providing positive control and explaining diauxic growth. Operator control here is protein-DNA binding, not methylation.

questions.q: Which technique amplifies a specific DNA segment exponentially in vitro using thermostable polymerase and primers?
questions.why: PCR cycles denaturation near 95 C, primer annealing near 55 C, and extension near 72 C with Taq polymerase, doubling target copies each cycle. Southern blotting detects specific DNA sequences already present using a labeled probe but does not amplify. Gel electrophoresis separates fragments by size and charge. Western blotting detects proteins with antibodies.

questions.q: A researcher wants to measure how much of a given mRNA is present in a tissue sample. Best method?
questions.why: RT-qPCR converts mRNA to cDNA and quantifies amplification in real time, giving transcript abundance. A Southern blot examines DNA, so it says nothing about transcript level. Karyotyping visualizes whole chromosomes and detects aneuploidy or large rearrangements. Sanger sequencing of genomic DNA reveals sequence, not expression level.

questions.q: Two genes are located 12 map units apart on the same chromosome. In a testcross, what percentage of offspring are expected to be recombinant?
questions.why: One map unit (centimorgan) equals one percent recombination, so 12 map units predicts 12 percent recombinant offspring, split between the two recombinant classes. Fifty percent indicates unlinked genes or loci far enough apart that crossing over occurs in essentially every meiosis. Twenty-four percent doubles the map distance incorrectly. Six percent is the expected frequency of each single recombinant class, not of both combined.

questions.q: Which cross demonstrates incomplete dominance rather than codominance?
choices: Red and white parents producing pink offspring with intermediate pigment
I-A and I-B alleles both expressed on the red cell surface
MN blood group offspring expressing both M and N antigens
Roan cattle with distinct red and white hairs in the same coat
questions.why: Incomplete dominance produces a blended intermediate phenotype because one functional allele yields only half the product, as in pink snapdragons. AB blood type is codominance because both antigens are fully and separately expressed. The MN blood group is a classic codominant system for the same reason. Roan coat color is codominance too, since both colors appear side by side rather than blending.

questions.q: A trait is determined by two genes where the homozygous recessive genotype at one locus masks expression at the other. This is:
questions.why: Epistasis is interaction between separate loci in which one gene's genotype masks another's, classically altering the 9:3:3:1 dihybrid ratio to 9:3:4 or 9:7. Pleiotropy is the reverse relationship, one gene affecting many traits. Polygenic inheritance means many loci each add small additive effects, giving continuous variation. Linkage disequilibrium is non-random association of alleles at nearby loci in a population, not a masking interaction.

questions.q: A carrier mother of an X-linked recessive disease has children with an unaffected father. What fraction of their sons are expected to be affected?
questions.why: Each son receives one of the mother's two X chromosomes at random, so half get the mutant allele and, having no second X, are affected. Zero would apply only if the mother were not a carrier. One quarter is the fraction of all children, not of sons, who are affected males. All sons would be affected only if the mother were homozygous for the mutant allele.

questions.q: Females heterozygous for an X-linked trait may show patchy expression such as mosaic retinal or skin findings because of:
choices: Random X inactivation early in embryogenesis (lyonization)
Imprinting of the paternal X in all tissues
Somatic recombination between X and Y
questions.why: One X is randomly inactivated as a Barr body in each cell early in development, and that choice is clonally inherited, so tissue becomes a mosaic of cells expressing either allele. Nondisjunction produces aneuploid cells, not mosaic allele expression in a euploid female. Paternal X imprinting is uniform in marsupials and in human placenta but not the mechanism of somatic mosaicism in human tissues. X-Y recombination is limited to small pseudoautosomal regions and does not cause this pattern.

questions.q: During which stage of meiosis does crossing over between homologous chromosomes occur?
questions.why: Homologs synapse and form chiasmata in prophase I (pachytene), and this recombination generates new allele combinations. Metaphase II aligns sister chromatids of already-haploid cells at the plate. Anaphase II separates sister chromatids, analogous to mitotic anaphase. Telophase I follows separation of homologs, after crossing over is complete.

questions.q: Nondisjunction in meiosis II produces gametes with which composition?
choices: Two different homologs of one chromosome plus normal complement
Two identical sister chromatids of one chromosome, with other gametes lacking it
A full diploid set in every gamete
A balanced translocation in half the gametes
questions.why: Meiosis II failure separates homologs normally but not sister chromatids, so one gamete gets two copies of the same chromatid and another gets none, while the other two gametes are normal. Two different homologs in one gamete indicates meiosis I nondisjunction. A fully diploid gamete would require failure of both divisions. Balanced translocations arise from structural rearrangement, not nondisjunction.

questions.q: A tall adolescent male has small firm testes, gynecomastia, and elevated FSH and LH with low testosterone. Most likely karyotype?
questions.why: Klinefelter syndrome, 47,XXY, causes seminiferous tubule dysgenesis and Leydig cell dysfunction, so testosterone falls while gonadotropins rise and aromatized estrogen produces gynecomastia. SRY deletion in a 46,XY individual yields a female phenotype with streak gonads. 45,X is Turner syndrome, a female phenotype with short stature. 47,XYY males are typically tall with normal fertility and normal hormone levels.

questions.q: Which statement about penetrance and expressivity is correct?
choices: Penetrance describes severity in affected individuals
Expressivity describes the proportion of carriers showing any phenotype
Penetrance is all-or-none across carriers; expressivity is how severe the phenotype is in those affected
Both terms refer only to recessive conditions
questions.why: Penetrance is the fraction of genotype carriers who show any phenotype, a yes-or-no measure across a population, while expressivity grades severity among those who do show it, as in the range of Marfan features. The first and second options swap the two definitions. Both concepts apply to dominant conditions most visibly, such as BRCA1 mutations with incomplete penetrance, so restricting them to recessive traits is wrong.

questions.q: A couple has one child with cystic fibrosis. Neither parent is affected. What is the chance their next child is affected?
questions.why: Both parents must be obligate carriers, so each pregnancy independently carries a 1/4 risk; prior outcomes do not change the odds. One half would apply if one parent were affected and the other a carrier. Two thirds is the carrier probability for an unaffected sibling of an affected child. One eighth would require an additional 1/2 conditional factor that does not exist once carrier status is established.

questions.q: Which molecular defect underlies sickle cell disease?
choices: A missense mutation replacing glutamate with valine at position 6 of beta-globin
A trinucleotide repeat expansion in the beta-globin promoter
questions.why: A single A to T change gives valine in place of glutamate at beta-globin position 6, creating a hydrophobic patch that lets deoxygenated HbS polymerize into fibers that deform the cell. Alpha-globin deletions cause alpha-thalassemia, a quantitative rather than qualitative defect. Nonsense mutations in beta-globin cause beta-thalassemia by eliminating chain production. Trinucleotide repeat expansions cause Huntington disease and fragile X, not hemoglobinopathies.

questions.q: Why does sickle cell trait persist at high frequency in regions with endemic falciparum malaria?
choices: Genetic drift in small isolated populations
Heterozygote advantage, since HbAS carriers have reduced severe malaria mortality
A higher mutation rate at the beta-globin locus in those regions
questions.why: Balancing selection maintains the allele because heterozygotes survive severe malaria better than either homozygote, a textbook heterozygote advantage. Drift produces random frequency changes and would not reproduce the same pattern independently across several malarial regions. Mutation rates are not elevated by environmental malaria exposure and are far too low to maintain these frequencies. Gene flow from non-endemic populations would dilute rather than sustain the allele.

questions.q: In a small isolated founding population, an uncommon allele reaches unusually high frequency. This is best explained by:
choices: Founder effect, a form of genetic drift
questions.why: When a few individuals establish a population, their allele frequencies become the new baseline by chance, which explains Tay-Sachs among Ashkenazi Jews and Ellis-van Creveld among the Old Order Amish. Selection requires a fitness advantage, which is absent for most of these disease alleles. Mutation is far too slow to raise an allele frequency in a few generations. Assortative mating changes genotype proportions but not allele frequencies.

questions.q: Gel electrophoresis separates DNA fragments primarily on what basis?
choices: Base composition, with GC-rich fragments moving faster
Charge only, since fragments differ in net charge
Sequence specificity to an immobilized probe
Size, with smaller fragments migrating farther through the gel matrix
questions.why: The uniform negative charge per unit length of DNA means charge-to-mass ratio is nearly constant, so the sieving gel separates by length, with small fragments traveling farthest toward the anode. GC content affects melting temperature, not standard migration. Charge alone cannot separate DNA because it scales with length. Probe hybridization is the step that follows transfer in a Southern blot, not the separation principle.

questions.q: CRISPR-Cas9 achieves targeted genome editing because:
choices: A guide RNA base-pairs with a genomic sequence adjacent to a PAM and directs Cas9 to cut there
Cas9 randomly nicks DNA until the desired mutation occurs
The system inserts a retroviral vector at any transcriptionally active site
Cas9 recognizes methylated cytosine residues and excises them
questions.why: Specificity comes from roughly 20 nucleotides of guide RNA complementarity plus a required protospacer adjacent motif; the double-strand break is then repaired by error-prone NHEJ to knock out a gene or by homology-directed repair to knock in a sequence. Cas9 does not cut randomly; that would be useless for editing. Retroviral vectors integrate semi-randomly and are a separate gene-transfer method. Methylcytosine excision is base-excision repair chemistry, unrelated to Cas9 targeting.

questions.q: A tumor suppressor gene typically causes cancer by which genetic mechanism?
choices: A single gain-of-function mutation acting dominantly
Loss of function of both alleles, following the two-hit hypothesis
Amplification of the gene to many copies
Translocation placing it under a strong promoter
questions.why: Tumor suppressors such as RB1 and TP53 restrain the cell cycle, so both copies must be lost for control to fail; inherited cancer syndromes start with one germline hit and need only one somatic hit. A single dominant gain of function describes oncogenes such as mutant RAS. Amplification is an oncogene mechanism, as with HER2 and MYC. Promoter translocation is also an oncogene mechanism, exemplified by MYC in Burkitt lymphoma.

questions.q: Which statement about the genetic code is correct?
choices: Each amino acid is specified by exactly one codon
Codons overlap, so one base can belong to two codons
It is degenerate, so most amino acids have more than one codon, largely varying at the third base
It differs completely between bacteria and humans
questions.why: Sixty-one sense codons encode twenty amino acids, so degeneracy exists and wobble at the third position means many such substitutions are silent. One codon per amino acid would leave no redundancy and contradicts the 64-codon table. The code is non-overlapping and read in successive triplets from a fixed start. It is nearly universal, which is what makes bacterial expression of human proteins possible, with only small exceptions such as mitochondrial codons.

questions.q: A DNA polymerase lacking 3-prime to 5-prime exonuclease activity would most likely cause:
choices: Failure to unwind the double helix
Loss of telomere length with each division
An elevated rate of point mutations from uncorrected misincorporations
questions.why: The 3-prime to 5-prime exonuclease is the proofreading function that excises mismatched nucleotides immediately after insertion, raising fidelity roughly a hundredfold; losing it produces a mutator phenotype. Unwinding is done by helicase, not polymerase. Okazaki fragment joining requires DNA ligase after RNase H and polymerase fill-in. Telomere shortening reflects the end-replication problem and telomerase activity, not proofreading.

questions.q: In a dihybrid cross of two heterozygotes for unlinked genes (AaBb x AaBb), what fraction of offspring show both recessive phenotypes?
questions.why: Independent assortment gives a 9:3:3:1 ratio, and the double recessive aabb class is 1/4 times 1/4, or 1/16. The 3/16 classes show one dominant and one recessive trait. The 9/16 class shows both dominant phenotypes. One quarter is the probability of being homozygous recessive at a single locus, ignoring the second gene.

questions.q: Which amino acid property best explains why leucine, isoleucine and valine cluster in a protein's interior?
choices: Nonpolar aliphatic side chains driven inward by the hydrophobic effect
A side chain that acts as a strong hydrogen bond donor
questions.why: Branched aliphatic side chains cannot hydrogen bond with water, so burying them increases solvent entropy, the main driving force of protein folding. Negative charge belongs to aspartate and glutamate, which favor the surface. Disulfide bridges form only between cysteine residues. Strong hydrogen bond donors such as serine, threonine and asparagine are typically surface-exposed or involved in specific internal networks.

questions.q: An enzyme has a pH optimum of 7.4 and loses activity at pH 2. The most likely reason is:
choices: Protonation of catalytic and structural side chains, disrupting ionic interactions and denaturing the active site
Depletion of ATP in the assay
Formation of additional disulfide bonds at low pH
questions.why: Extreme acid protonates carboxylates and histidine imidazoles, destroying the salt bridges and precise charge arrangement the active site needs, so catalysis fails. Substrate modification would change the reaction, not the enzyme's pH profile. ATP is irrelevant unless the enzyme is a kinase and was not part of this description. Low pH does not promote disulfide bond formation; oxidizing conditions and free cysteine thiols do.

questions.q: In Michaelis-Menten kinetics, what does Km represent?
choices: The maximum reaction rate at saturating substrate
The turnover number of the enzyme
The substrate concentration at which the reaction runs at half of Vmax, an inverse index of apparent affinity
The concentration of enzyme needed to reach Vmax
questions.why: Km is the substrate concentration giving half-maximal velocity; a low Km means the enzyme reaches half speed at low substrate and thus binds tightly. Vmax is the plateau rate, a separate parameter that depends on enzyme concentration. The turnover number kcat equals Vmax divided by total enzyme. Km is a property of the enzyme-substrate pair and does not change with enzyme concentration.

questions.q: A competitive inhibitor added to an enzyme assay will produce which change?
choices: Increased apparent Km with unchanged Vmax
questions.why: A competitive inhibitor binds the active site and can be outcompeted, so enough substrate still reaches Vmax while more substrate is needed for half-maximal rate, raising apparent Km. Reduced Vmax with unchanged Km describes noncompetitive inhibition. Reduced Vmax with reduced Km describes uncompetitive inhibition, which binds only the ES complex. No inhibitor increases Vmax.

questions.q: Hemoglobin's sigmoidal oxygen binding curve reflects which property absent from myoglobin?
choices: Cooperative binding among four subunits, where oxygen binding at one heme raises affinity at the others
Covalent bonding of oxygen to the heme iron
The presence of a copper cofactor
questions.why: Hemoglobin is a tetramer that shifts from the low-affinity T state to the high-affinity R state as oxygen binds, producing the sigmoid curve that allows loading in lung and unloading in tissue. Myoglobin is a monomer with a hyperbolic curve and higher affinity, suiting it to storage. Oxygen binds reversibly and coordinately, not covalently, to ferrous iron in both proteins. Copper is a cofactor in cytochrome c oxidase and hemocyanin, not hemoglobin.

questions.q: A rise in 2,3-bisphosphoglycerate, CO2, or temperature shifts the oxyhemoglobin curve which way and with what effect?
choices: Left, increasing oxygen affinity and tissue delivery
Right, decreasing oxygen affinity and improving unloading in tissue
Left, decreasing oxygen affinity and impairing loading in the lung
No shift, since these factors affect only myoglobin
questions.why: These are markers of metabolically active or hypoxic tissue; they stabilize the T state, shift the curve right and release more oxygen at a given PO2, which is the Bohr effect. A left shift raises affinity and impairs unloading, as with fetal hemoglobin, alkalosis or hypothermia. The third option mixes direction and effect incorrectly, since left shift means increased affinity. Myoglobin lacks the allosteric sites these effectors use.

questions.q: Which enzyme catalyzes the committed, rate-limiting step of glycolysis?
questions.why: PFK-1 converts fructose-6-phosphate to fructose-1,6-bisphosphate, the first step committed to glycolysis; it is inhibited by ATP and citrate and activated by AMP and fructose-2,6-bisphosphate. Hexokinase traps glucose but glucose-6-phosphate can still enter glycogen or the pentose phosphate pathway. Glucose-6-phosphatase belongs to gluconeogenesis in liver and kidney. Pyruvate kinase is regulated but acts at the end of the pathway, after commitment.

questions.q: What is the net ATP and NADH yield of glycolysis per glucose under aerobic conditions?
questions.why: Two ATP are invested and four are produced by substrate-level phosphorylation, giving a net of two, and glyceraldehyde-3-phosphate dehydrogenase reduces two NAD-plus per glucose. Four ATP is the gross figure before subtracting the investment phase. Four NADH per glucose is the yield from the TCA cycle turns plus pyruvate dehydrogenase, not from glycolysis. One ATP and two NADH understates the ATP yield.

questions.q: Under anaerobic conditions in skeletal muscle, why must pyruvate be reduced to lactate?
choices: To regenerate NAD-plus so glyceraldehyde-3-phosphate dehydrogenase can continue
To generate additional ATP directly from lactate dehydrogenase
To supply acetyl-CoA for the TCA cycle
To remove excess oxygen from the cytosol
questions.why: Without oxygen the electron transport chain cannot reoxidize NADH, so lactate dehydrogenase regenerates cytosolic NAD-plus and lets glycolysis and its two net ATP continue. Lactate dehydrogenase produces no ATP itself. Acetyl-CoA is made by pyruvate dehydrogenase, which is inhibited under anaerobic conditions by rising NADH and acetyl-CoA. There is no mechanism or need to remove oxygen from the cytosol.

questions.q: Which cofactor is NOT required by the pyruvate dehydrogenase complex?
questions.why: Pyruvate dehydrogenase uses thiamine pyrophosphate, lipoic acid, CoA, FAD and NAD-plus, the classic five; biotin is not among them. Biotin is the carboxyl carrier for pyruvate carboxylase, acetyl-CoA carboxylase and propionyl-CoA carboxylase. Lipoic acid transfers the acetyl group and is the target of arsenic poisoning. FAD on dihydrolipoyl dehydrogenase reoxidizes lipoamide and passes electrons to NAD-plus.

questions.q: Which TCA cycle step produces GTP (or ATP) by substrate-level phosphorylation?
questions.why: Succinyl-CoA synthetase captures the energy of the thioester bond to phosphorylate GDP to GTP, the only substrate-level phosphorylation in the cycle. Citrate synthase condenses acetyl-CoA with oxaloacetate and is exergonic but produces no nucleotide triphosphate. Isocitrate dehydrogenase is the rate-limiting step and yields NADH and CO2. Malate dehydrogenase yields NADH and regenerates oxaloacetate.

questions.q: One turn of the TCA cycle from one acetyl-CoA yields which set of products?
questions.why: Isocitrate dehydrogenase, alpha-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase and malate dehydrogenase each give one NADH; succinate dehydrogenase gives FADH2; succinyl-CoA synthetase gives GTP; and two decarboxylations release two CO2. Two NADH omits one dehydrogenase step. Two FADH2 and two GTP double steps that occur once per turn. Four NADH and three CO2 would describe a turn plus pyruvate dehydrogenase, which is not part of the cycle itself.

questions.q: In oxidative phosphorylation, what directly drives ATP synthesis by ATP synthase?
choices: Direct transfer of phosphate from NADH to ADP
The proton motive force across the inner mitochondrial membrane
questions.why: Complexes I, III and IV pump protons into the intermembrane space, and the resulting electrochemical gradient drives protons back through ATP synthase, rotating the F0 unit and forcing ADP phosphorylation. NADH donates electrons to complex I, not phosphate to ADP. Acetyl-CoA thioester energy is captured within the TCA cycle, not at ATP synthase. Substrate-level phosphorylation is a separate, gradient-independent mechanism.

questions.q: 2,4-dinitrophenol causes hyperthermia and weight loss because it acts as:
choices: An uncoupler that carries protons across the inner membrane, dissipating the gradient as heat
A complex IV inhibitor blocking electron flow to oxygen
An inhibitor of the adenine nucleotide translocase
questions.why: Uncouplers shuttle protons back into the matrix without passing through ATP synthase, so electron transport and oxygen consumption accelerate while the energy is released as heat rather than ATP, exactly like physiologic thermogenin in brown fat. Complex IV inhibitors such as cyanide and carbon monoxide stop oxygen consumption entirely. Oligomycin inhibits ATP synthase and secondarily halts electron transport. Atractyloside blocks the ADP/ATP translocase without directly generating heat this way.

questions.q: Cyanide poisoning is lethal because it does what?
choices: Binds ferric iron in cytochrome c oxidase, halting electron transfer to oxygen
Opens a proton leak in the inner membrane
questions.why: Cyanide binds the a3 heme iron of complex IV, so electrons cannot reach oxygen, the chain backs up, oxidative phosphorylation stops, and venous oxygen stays high because tissue cannot extract it. Glycolysis continues and produces lactate, which is why lactic acidosis is the hallmark. A proton leak describes uncouplers, which increase rather than abolish oxygen use. Glucose transport is unaffected.

questions.q: Which enzyme catalyzes the committed step of fatty acid synthesis and is stimulated by insulin and citrate?
questions.why: Acetyl-CoA carboxylase uses biotin and ATP to make malonyl-CoA, the committed step; citrate activates it in the fed state and AMP-activated kinase phosphorylates and inhibits it when energy is low. Carnitine palmitoyltransferase I moves fatty acids into mitochondria for oxidation and is inhibited by malonyl-CoA. Fatty acid synthase elongates the chain after commitment. Hormone-sensitive lipase mobilizes stored triglyceride during fasting and is opposed by insulin.

questions.q: Long-chain fatty acids require carnitine for which step of beta-oxidation?
choices: Activation to acyl-CoA in the cytosol
Transport across the inner mitochondrial membrane
questions.why: The inner mitochondrial membrane is impermeable to long-chain acyl-CoA, so CPT-I exchanges CoA for carnitine, a translocase carries acylcarnitine in, and CPT-II regenerates acyl-CoA in the matrix. Activation by acyl-CoA synthetase happens on the outer mitochondrial membrane and does not need carnitine. The FAD-linked dehydrogenation and the final thiolysis both occur in the matrix after transport is complete.

questions.q: During prolonged fasting, hepatic ketone body production rises chiefly because:
choices: Excess dietary carbohydrate overloads the TCA cycle
Muscle secretes ketones into the blood
Oxaloacetate is diverted to gluconeogenesis, so acetyl-CoA from beta-oxidation accumulates
questions.why: Fasting drives gluconeogenesis, consuming oxaloacetate, so acetyl-CoA from rapid beta-oxidation cannot enter the TCA cycle and is condensed into acetoacetate and beta-hydroxybutyrate for use by brain and muscle. Carbohydrate excess suppresses ketogenesis by raising insulin. Insulin does inhibit hormone-sensitive lipase, but insulin is low in fasting, which is why lipolysis accelerates. Muscle consumes ketones and lacks the thiophorase arrangement needed to release them; only liver exports them.

questions.q: Which lipoprotein carries dietary triglycerides from the intestine into lymph and then blood?
questions.why: Chylomicrons assemble in enterocytes around apoB-48, enter lacteals, and deliver dietary triglyceride to tissue via lipoprotein lipase activated by apoC-II. VLDL carries triglyceride made in the liver and uses apoB-100. LDL is the cholesterol-rich VLDL remnant taken up by the LDL receptor. HDL performs reverse cholesterol transport and supplies apoC-II and apoE to other particles.

questions.q: Statins lower LDL cholesterol primarily by which mechanism?
choices: Binding bile acids in the gut lumen
Inhibiting HMG-CoA reductase, which upregulates hepatic LDL receptors
Blocking intestinal cholesterol absorption at NPC1L1
questions.why: HMG-CoA reductase is the rate-limiting step of cholesterol synthesis; inhibiting it depletes hepatic cholesterol, and the liver responds by displaying more LDL receptors that clear LDL from plasma. Bile acid sequestrants act in the gut lumen and are a separate class. Ezetimibe blocks NPC1L1 absorption. Fibrates activate PPAR-alpha and increase lipoprotein lipase activity, lowering triglycerides more than LDL.

questions.q: In the urea cycle, which molecule donates the second nitrogen incorporated into urea?
questions.why: Argininosuccinate synthetase condenses citrulline with aspartate, and that aspartate nitrogen becomes the second nitrogen of urea; the first arrives as ammonia through carbamoyl phosphate synthetase I. Glutamine transports ammonia in blood and donates nitrogen in the mitochondrion indirectly, but it is not the direct donor in the cycle. Alanine carries nitrogen from muscle to liver in the glucose-alanine cycle and is transaminated first. Glycine supplies nitrogen for heme and purine synthesis, not urea directly.

questions.q: An infant with an ornithine transcarbamylase deficiency presents with lethargy, vomiting, hyperammonemia and respiratory alkalosis. Which laboratory finding is expected?
choices: Low orotic acid with high citrulline
Elevated orotic acid with low citrulline and no acidosis
questions.why: OTC deficiency is X-linked and blocks conversion of ornithine and carbamoyl phosphate to citrulline, so citrulline is low while accumulated carbamoyl phosphate spills into pyrimidine synthesis and raises orotic acid, without the acidosis of organic acidemias. BUN falls rather than rises because urea cannot be made. High citrulline with normal orotic acid suggests a block further down, as in citrullinemia. Anion gap ketoacidosis points to an organic acidemia such as propionic acidemia.

questions.q: Which vitamin serves as the precursor of the coenzyme that carries one-carbon units in thymidylate and purine synthesis?
questions.why: Tetrahydrofolate derivatives donate one-carbon groups for dTMP and purine synthesis, which is why deficiency produces megaloblastic anemia and why methotrexate blocks dihydrofolate reductase. Niacin becomes NAD and NADP, redox carriers rather than one-carbon carriers. Riboflavin becomes FAD and FMN, also redox cofactors. Pyridoxine becomes pyridoxal phosphate, the cofactor for transamination, decarboxylation and glycogen phosphorylase.

questions.q: A patient with alcohol use disorder develops confusion, ophthalmoplegia and ataxia. Deficiency of which cofactor explains the findings?
choices: Thiamine, cofactor for pyruvate dehydrogenase, alpha-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase and transketolase
Vitamin K, cofactor for gamma-glutamyl carboxylase
questions.why: Thiamine pyrophosphate deficiency cripples oxidative decarboxylation and the pentose phosphate transketolase reaction, starving highly aerobic brain regions and producing Wernicke encephalopathy, which is why glucose without thiamine can precipitate it. B12 deficiency causes megaloblastic anemia with subacute combined degeneration, not ophthalmoplegia. Vitamin C deficiency causes scurvy with poor wound healing and perifollicular hemorrhage. Vitamin K deficiency causes bleeding from defective clotting factors.

questions.q: Which statement about the pentose phosphate pathway is correct?
choices: It generates ATP by substrate-level phosphorylation
It occurs in mitochondria and produces FADH2
Its oxidative phase generates NADPH and ribose-5-phosphate, with glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase as the rate-limiting step
It consumes NADPH to reduce glutathione
questions.why: The oxidative branch is cytosolic and irreversible, producing two NADPH and ribulose-5-phosphate, and G6PD is rate-limiting and inhibited by NADPH. The pathway makes no ATP. It is cytosolic and produces no FADH2. It supplies rather than consumes NADPH; glutathione reductase then spends that NADPH, which is why G6PD deficiency causes oxidative hemolysis.

questions.q: A patient develops hemolysis with bite cells and Heinz bodies after starting primaquine. The underlying defect is:
choices: Pyruvate kinase deficiency reducing red cell ATP
Glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase deficiency limiting NADPH for glutathione regeneration
questions.why: Without adequate NADPH, reduced glutathione cannot be regenerated, so oxidant drugs, fava beans or infection denature hemoglobin into Heinz bodies that splenic macrophages pit, producing bite cells. Pyruvate kinase deficiency causes chronic nonspherocytic hemolysis without oxidant triggers or Heinz bodies. Spherocytosis shows spherocytes, increased osmotic fragility and a positive response to splenectomy. Sickle cell disease shows sickled forms triggered by hypoxia and dehydration rather than oxidant drugs.

questions.q: Which hormone-driven change best characterizes the fed state in the liver?
choices: Insulin promotes glycogen synthase activity and dephosphorylation of glycogen phosphorylase
Glucagon activates protein kinase A and stimulates glycogenolysis
Epinephrine mobilizes fatty acids from adipose tissue
questions.why: Insulin activates protein phosphatase 1, which dephosphorylates glycogen synthase to its active form and glycogen phosphorylase to its inactive form, storing glucose. Glucagon signaling through PKA is the fasting response and does the opposite. Epinephrine drives lipolysis in stress and fasting. Cortisol upregulates PEPCK and other gluconeogenic enzymes during prolonged fasting and stress.

questions.q: Which enzyme is unique to gluconeogenesis and allows bypass of the pyruvate kinase step?
questions.why: Pyruvate carboxylase makes oxaloacetate using biotin and ATP, and PEPCK converts it to phosphoenolpyruvate using GTP, together bypassing the irreversible pyruvate kinase reaction. Hexokinase and PFK-1 are glycolytic enzymes whose steps are bypassed by glucose-6-phosphatase and fructose-1,6-bisphosphatase respectively. Aldolase catalyzes a reversible step shared by both pathways.

questions.q: A child has hepatomegaly, fasting hypoglycemia, lactic acidosis and hyperuricemia, with normal response of glycogen structure. Most likely deficiency?
questions.why: Von Gierke disease (type I) blocks the final step releasing free glucose, so glucose-6-phosphate accumulates, driving glycolysis to lactate and the pentose pathway toward urate retention, with severe fasting hypoglycemia and a large liver. Acid alpha-glucosidase deficiency is Pompe disease, dominated by cardiomegaly and hypotonia rather than hypoglycemia. Muscle phosphorylase deficiency is McArdle disease, with exercise intolerance and no hypoglycemia. Debranching deficiency (Cori disease) causes milder hypoglycemia with abnormal limit dextrin structure and normal lactate.

questions.q: Phenylketonuria causes intellectual disability if untreated because of which mechanism?
choices: Accumulation of galactitol in the lens
Phenylalanine hydroxylase deficiency causing phenylalanine buildup and tyrosine deficiency
questions.why: Loss of phenylalanine hydroxylase (or its BH4 cofactor) raises phenylalanine, which is shunted to phenylketones and competes for the large neutral amino acid transporter at the blood-brain barrier, while tyrosine becomes essential, limiting catecholamine and melanin synthesis and producing fair skin. Galactitol accumulation causes cataracts in galactosemia. Branched-chain ketoacid dehydrogenase deficiency causes maple syrup urine disease. Homocystinuria produces lens dislocation, marfanoid habitus and thrombosis.

questions.q: Which describes the primary structure of a protein?
choices: The linear sequence of amino acids joined by peptide bonds
Local folding into alpha helices and beta sheets stabilized by backbone hydrogen bonds
The three-dimensional fold of a single polypeptide
questions.why: Primary structure is sequence alone, determined by the gene and the only level held together by covalent peptide bonds (plus disulfides). Alpha helices and beta sheets are secondary structure. The overall fold of one chain is tertiary structure, stabilized by hydrophobic packing, hydrogen bonds, ionic interactions and disulfides. Multi-subunit assembly, as in hemoglobin, is quaternary structure.

questions.q: An enzyme reaction shows sigmoidal rather than hyperbolic kinetics. This most likely indicates:
choices: An allosteric enzyme with cooperative subunit interactions
That the enzyme is operating below its Km
The presence of a competitive inhibitor
questions.why: Sigmoidal curves arise when binding at one site changes affinity at others, as in aspartate transcarbamoylase and phosphofructokinase-1, which makes these enzymes sensitive switches at physiologic substrate levels. Covalent inhibition lowers Vmax and does not create sigmoidicity. Operating below Km describes a position on a curve, not its shape. Competitive inhibition shifts a hyperbolic curve rightward while keeping it hyperbolic.

questions.q: Which statement about enzyme catalysis is correct?
choices: Enzymes make unfavorable reactions favorable by changing delta G
Enzymes are consumed stoichiometrically during the reaction
Enzymes lower activation energy by stabilizing the transition state, without altering the equilibrium constant
questions.why: Catalysts speed both forward and reverse reactions equally by stabilizing the transition state, so rate rises while delta G and Keq stay fixed. Enzymes cannot make a thermodynamically unfavorable reaction favorable, though coupling to ATP hydrolysis can. Enzymes are regenerated and act catalytically at low concentration. Because both directions accelerate equally, equilibrium position is unchanged.

questions.q: Which buffer system is most important for minute-to-minute pH control in extracellular fluid?
choices: Phosphate buffer, because its pKa is closest to 7.4
Bicarbonate-carbonic acid, because CO2 is volatile and independently regulated by ventilation
questions.why: Despite a pKa near 6.1, the bicarbonate system dominates because the lungs can blow off CO2 within minutes and the kidney adjusts bicarbonate, making it an open system. Phosphate has a favorable pKa near 6.8 but its extracellular concentration is low, so it matters more inside cells and in urine. Ammonia buffering is a renal tubular mechanism, not a plasma one. Hemoglobin is a major buffer but it is intracellular within erythrocytes, not a plasma protein.

questions.q: Which vitamin functions as the cofactor for transamination reactions catalyzed by ALT and AST?
questions.why: Pyridoxal phosphate forms a Schiff base with the amino acid and shuttles the amino group to alpha-ketoglutarate, and B6 also supports decarboxylations, heme synthesis and glycogen phosphorylase, which is why isoniazid-induced B6 deficiency causes neuropathy and sideroblastic anemia. TPP serves oxidative decarboxylation and transketolase. Biotin carries carboxyl groups in carboxylase reactions. Cobalamin serves methylmalonyl-CoA mutase and methionine synthase.

questions.q: Vitamin C deficiency causes poor wound healing and bleeding gums because ascorbate is required to:
choices: Carboxylate glutamate residues in clotting factors
Hydroxylate proline and lysine residues for collagen triple-helix cross-linking
Transfer methyl groups in homocysteine metabolism
Reduce coenzyme Q in the electron transport chain
questions.why: Prolyl and lysyl hydroxylases need ascorbate to keep their iron reduced; without it collagen cannot form stable cross-linked triple helices, so vessels and healing tissue are fragile. Gamma-carboxylation of glutamate is a vitamin K-dependent reaction. Methyl transfer in homocysteine metabolism depends on folate and B12. Coenzyme Q reduction is carried out by complexes I and II, not by ascorbate.

questions.q: A patient with untreated pernicious anemia has elevated methylmalonic acid and homocysteine. Which deficiency is present?
choices: Vitamin B12 deficiency from loss of intrinsic factor
questions.why: B12 is required by methylmalonyl-CoA mutase and by methionine synthase, so both methylmalonic acid and homocysteine rise, and the accumulated methylmalonyl-CoA disrupts myelin, producing neurologic findings. Folate deficiency raises homocysteine but leaves methylmalonic acid normal, which is the key discriminator. Iron deficiency causes microcytic anemia without these metabolite changes. B6 deficiency causes sideroblastic anemia and neuropathy without elevated methylmalonic acid.

questions.q: Which describes the role of ATP hydrolysis in coupled biochemical reactions?
choices: It catalyzes reactions by lowering activation energy
It provides a large negative free energy change that drives an otherwise unfavorable reaction forward
It donates electrons to reduce substrates
It raises the equilibrium constant of the unfavorable reaction itself
questions.why: ATP hydrolysis releases about 7.3 kcal per mole under standard conditions and more in cells, so summing the two reactions yields a net negative delta G, as when hexokinase couples phosphorylation to glucose trapping. Lowering activation energy is the job of the enzyme, not of ATP. Electron donation comes from NADH, NADPH and FADH2. The coupled overall reaction becomes favorable, but the intrinsic Keq of the unfavorable half-reaction does not change.

questions.q: Why do the NADH produced in glycolysis yield less ATP than mitochondrial NADH?
choices: Cytosolic NADH is oxidized more slowly by complex I
Cytosolic NADH is degraded before it can be used
The glycerol phosphate shuttle delivers electrons to FAD, entering at complex II and bypassing one proton-pumping site
Cytosolic NADH carries only one electron
questions.why: The inner membrane is impermeable to NADH, so in muscle and brain the glycerol-3-phosphate shuttle hands electrons to FAD, entering downstream of complex I and giving roughly 1.5 ATP instead of 2.5; the malate-aspartate shuttle in liver and heart preserves the full yield. Rate of oxidation by complex I is not the issue, since cytosolic NADH never reaches complex I. Cytosolic NADH is not degraded; it is shuttled. All NADH carries two electrons.

questions.q: Which feature of the phospholipid bilayer accounts for its spontaneous formation in water?
choices: Uniform positive charge on the head groups
Saturated tails locking into a rigid crystal
Amphipathic molecules that bury hydrophobic tails and expose polar head groups to water
questions.why: Each phospholipid has a polar head and two nonpolar tails, so bilayer formation maximizes water's hydrogen bonding and entropy, the same hydrophobic effect that folds proteins. No covalent bonds link adjacent phospholipids; the membrane is held by noncovalent forces and is fluid. Head groups vary in charge and many are zwitterionic or negative, not uniformly positive. Unsaturated tails with cis double bonds keep the membrane fluid rather than crystalline, and cholesterol buffers that fluidity.
